# AutoPrompt: Eliciting Knowledge from Language Models with Automatically Generated Prompts

**AutoPrompt** · EMNLP 2020

Read: [PDF](https://arxiv.org/pdf/2010.15980) · [arXiv](https://arxiv.org/abs/2010.15980) · [DOI](https://doi.org/10.18653/v1/2020.emnlp-main.346)  
Code: [autoprompt](https://github.com/ucinlp/autoprompt)

<p class="notice">An AI-written summary for orientation, not a source: check the original paper before relying on anything here.</p>

## In brief

- Searches discrete trigger tokens that elicit knowledge from masked language models.
- Gradient-guided token search.
- The white-box predecessor of the LLM-proposer optimizers below: it needs the model's gradients, and its prompts "lack interpretability" (§7).

## In plain words

Measuring what a pretrained language model knows is hard. Small classifiers trained on its internal representations add parameters of their own and can report knowledge that isn't there, and hand-written fill-in-the-blank prompts take guesswork, while models are "highly sensitive to this context" (§1). The authors build AutoPrompt, which turns a task into a fill-in-the-blank sentence for a masked language model (a model trained to fill in hidden words; here BERT and RoBERTa) and picks the extra words of that sentence automatically, by a search guided by the model's gradients; the model's weights never change (abstract, §2). With a found prompt, RoBERTa reaches 91.4% accuracy on a movie-review sentiment test set, against 85.2% with a hand-written prompt and 96.7% for a finetuned RoBERTa taken from a public leaderboard (Tab. 1). On the LAMA fact-retrieval test set, BERT's top guess is right for 43.3% of facts (averaged over relations), against 34.1% for the best earlier single prompt (§1, Tab. 4). The authors present this as automating manual prompt writing, calling the prompts "a viable parameter-free alternative to existing probing methods" (abstract).

## Background and terms

**Terms to know:** [mean reciprocal rank (MRR)](#/glossary/recallk-and-mean-reciprocal-rank-mrr) · [hyperparameter optimization](#/glossary/hyperparameter-optimization) · [masked language model (MLM)](#/glossary/masked-language-model) (here BERT-base, 110M parameters, and RoBERTa-large, 355M, §2.5) · precision@k (P@1, P@10) (§5 "Setup" doesn't define it; Tab. 4–5 report its mean).

**The paper's own terms:**
- **template, prompt**: the template places the task input, trigger tokens and one prediction slot `[P]` (a `[MASK]`) into the sentence fed to the MLM, the prompt (§2.1, Fig. 1).
- **trigger tokens** (`[T]`): words "shared across all prompts" of a task, found by the search (§2.2); per relation for facts (§5 "Setup", §6).
- **label tokens**: the words whose probabilities at the prediction slot are summed into one class's probability (§2.1, Eq. 1).
- **Original, T-REx, Original-RoBERTa**: the fact-retrieval test sets: LAMA's test set; a test split of the T-REx facts the authors gathered; and the LAMA facts whose answer is a single token for both models (§5).

**Builds on:**
- Wallace et al. (2019): AutoPrompt uses "a variant of the gradient-based search strategy proposed in Wallace et al. (2019)" (§1, §2.2).
- LAMA, Petroni et al. (2019): facts as cloze tests with hand-written prompts; the main baseline of §5–6.
- LPAQA, Jiang et al. (2020): prompts for the same facts "generated by mining Wikipedia, paraphrasing, and crowdsourcing" (§5).
- Probing classifiers (Conneau et al., 2018; Liu et al., 2019), set against prompting (§1).

## Problem and setting

- **The question:** "How can we directly evaluate the knowledge present in pretrained LMs, be it linguistic, factual, commonsense, or task-specific?" (§1).
  - sentiment: SST-2, the binary Stanford Sentiment Treebank of movie-review sentences (§3);
  - NLI: SICK-E, about 10,000 human-annotated sentence pairs, biased toward neutral, plus balanced 3-way and 2-way (contradiction vs entailment) variants (§4 "Setup");
  - fact retrieval: LAMA's 41 relations; training data is at most 1000 facts per relation from T-REx (facts that come "with context sentences", §6 "Setup"), topped up from Wikidata; proper nouns and gold answers of the training data can't be trigger tokens (§5 "Setup");
  - RE: T-REx facts with their context sentences, against a supervised RE model, with an evaluation modified "To make the evaluation fair for the supervised RE model" (§6 "Setup", App. B).
- **Correct means:** accuracy for sentiment and NLI; MRR, P@1 and P@10 on the true object's rank for facts (§5 "Setup"); in RE, the object's canonical form or its surface form "for any of the context sentences" (§6 "Setup").
- **Supervision:** labelled training data; each search returns its best prompt on development data (§2.5), the NLI and fact-retrieval search settings are chosen on development data too (§4–5 "Setup"), and scores come from "a separate withheld test set" (§2.5).

## Approach

- **Prediction (§2.1, Fig. 1):** a class's probability is the sum of the MLM's probabilities for its label tokens at the mask (Eq. 1). When labels are already words (entities), the most likely word is the prediction (Tab. 3).
- **Trigger search (§2.2):** triggers start as `[MASK]`. Each step estimates, for one trigger position, how much swapping in each vocabulary word would raise the log-likelihood of the correct label: a first-order approximation, the dot product of the word's input embedding with the gradient at that position (Eq. 2). The top-k words become candidates; each is re-scored, and the best prompt is kept. Finding candidates is "roughly as expensive as a single forward pass and backward pass of the model"; re-scoring "requires k forward passes".
- **Label tokens (§2.3):** for sentiment and NLI, a logistic classifier learns to predict the class from the MLM's hidden vector at the mask (Eqs. 3–4); every vocabulary word is then scored by feeding its output embedding to that classifier, and each class takes its top-k words (Eq. 5).
- **Loop (§2.5):** candidates come from one training batch and are compared on another; the best prompt on development data is returned.

## Results

- **Sentiment (§3, Tab. 1):** on SST-2's test set, RoBERTa with AutoPrompt scores 91.4 against 85.2 with the manual prompt "this movie was". Finetuned BERT (93.5), finetuned RoBERTa (96.7) and a BiLSTM with ELMo (89.3) are from the GLUE leaderboard (Tab. 1 caption). The authors read this as RoBERTa reaching "an accuracy on-par with finetuned BERT and ELMo models".
- **Low data (§3 "Accuracy in Low-Data Settings", Fig. 2):** development-set accuracy with 10, 100 and 1000 training examples, 10 runs each, against finetuning set up as Mosbach et al. (2020) recommend. The authors report that "finetuning outperforms" AutoPrompt on sentiment while AutoPrompt "can perform better than finetuning on NLI", and better average accuracy for both models with only 10 examples. RoBERTa's results are "more stable across all sample sizes", whereas finetuning "can result in “failed runs”". §1 states that AutoPrompt "achieves higher average- and worst-case accuracy than finetuning in low-data regimes".
- **NLI (§4, Tab. 2):** RoBERTa with AutoPrompt scores 69.3 on 3-way SICK-E, against 33.3 for the majority class, 49.4 for a RoBERTa linear probe and 84.0 for finetuned BERT; on 2-way, 87.3 against 95.6 for finetuned BERT. The authors call the 2-way result "comparable to a supervised finetuned BERT", and AutoPrompt's accuracy "comparable or higher" than linear probes'. With little data on 3-way, they report it "on par with finetuned BERT and significantly better than finetuned RoBERTa". Precision is highest on contradiction (§4 "MLMs Excel on Contradiction").
- **Fact retrieval (§5, Tab. 4):** on Original, BERT with 7 trigger tokens reaches P@1 43.34 against 31.10 for LAMA's prompts and 34.10 for LPAQA's best single prompt. The authors summarize this as "up to 12 points", and report beating LPAQA's ensemble of up to 30 prompts too. They conclude that BERT "contains more factual knowledge than previously estimated". AutoPrompt "performs especially well" for relations hard to phrase in natural language (§5 "Relation Breakdown"). On Original-RoBERTa, BERT slightly beats RoBERTa, whose prompts "tend to contain more irrelevant words" (Tab. 4 right).
- **Relation extraction (§6, Tab. 5):** BERT with AutoPrompt scores P@1 90.73 against 57.95 for the supervised model of Sorokin and Gurevych (2017), an LSTM relation encoder with attention (App. B); the authors call this "up to a 33% increase". On perturbed sentences, each object replaced by a random other object, BERT drops to 56.43 while the supervised model scores 58.81; the authors conclude "a significant portion of MLM accuracy comes from background information rather than relation extraction" (§6 "Perturbed Sentence Evaluation").

## Limits the authors state

- On "datasets such as QQP" (paraphrase detection) "and RTE" (textual entailment), "prompts generated manually and with" AutoPrompt "did not perform considerably better than chance" in a preliminary evaluation (§7).
- Prompt-based probes are "just one tool in the toolbox of the interpretability researcher" (§7).
- AutoPrompt needs labelled training data, as other probing techniques do, where manual prompts rely on "domain/language insights" (§7).
- Its prompts "lack interpretability" compared with human-designed ones (§7).
- It "can sometimes struggle when the training data is highly imbalanced"; the authors cite §4–5 for prompts that often just raise the majority label's likelihood, and say rebalancing "can help to mitigate this problem" (§7).
- Because of "the greedy search over the large discrete space of phrases", it "is sometimes brittle"; better crafting techniques are left "for future directions" (§7).
- Prompting is "a lower bound on a model's knowledge", so RoBERTa's lower relative performance "does not mean that the model actually knows less" (§5).

## Open problems and building blocks

- **Open:** why RoBERTa doesn't beat BERT on fact retrieval: "it is worthy of investigating this further in future work" (§5). The method "can be trivially extended to standard language models, and thus maybe useful for constructing inputs for models like GPT-3" (§8); the prediction token then "must occur at the end of the prompt" (§2, footnote 1).
- **Released:** an implementation that "supports prompt generation for pretrained models in the HuggingFace transformers library … on arbitrary datasets" (§2.5), and "Source code and datasets to reproduce the results" (§8).
- **To reuse it:** labelled training data (§7); gradients with respect to the input embeddings (§2.2). The SST-2 grid search "Required 2 days to run with 8 NVIDIA 2080Ti GPUs" (§3, footnote 3). Per task, "Only prompts are stored", not model checkpoints (§7).
